item.title: AI Avatars Seduced Me: A Therapist's Personal Experience
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Avatars Seduced Me: A Therapist's Personal Experience

A therapist describes how AI drew her in and how she re-established boundaries.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • AI bots and avatars can draw us into intimate relationships.
  • These relationships lead to isolation and loneliness.
  • There is no capacity in AI bots for conflict or self-awareness.
  • We need human relationships to feel human.

In my work as a supervisor, teacher, and consultant to other therapists, I have heard a lot of concerns about AI in therapy. A few of my own clients have consulted ChatGPT, Claude, and the myriad other online advisors, and we have frequently been able to integrate their experience into the work we are doing.

But other than asking ChatGPT for suggestions about titles for articles I’m working on, which is something I’m really bad at myself, and for ideas about activities for my visiting grandchildren, I’ve pretty much stayed away from AI.

Except, that is, for my love of the gamified language app “Duolingo.”

I never thought of the avatars as AI

Somehow, I never thought of the adorable characters and charming stories of the program as AI-generated. I admire the use of clever tools that keep me engaged, ensuring that I get 15-20 minutes of language learning a day, almost without trying. My Spanish vocabulary and conjugation skills are improving, and my ability to understand and converse with my Spanish-speaking clients and their interpreter in Spanish is a personal huge reward.

But recently, Duolingo offered a month of free video “conversations” with some of the avatars. Hesitant at first, mostly because I wasn’t sure that my language skills were up to the point where I could have conversations, I decided to try it. What did I have to lose?

People are having more intimate relationships with AI bots

It turned out that I quickly lost any sense of superiority I might have had over anyone drawn to AI. My avatar buddies are funny, personable, highly complimentary, and encouraging. These qualities are, of course, both what attracts people to AI and what many people worry about.

Esther Perel, a widely recognized relationship therapist, tells us in an interview, “People are having more and more intimate relationships with their AI bots.”

And in a thoughtful exploration of AI on his PT blog, Dr. Steven E. Hyler writes, “These systems appear to listen patiently and respond empathetically, and they remain available no matter what is said.”

I am charmed when the teenaged character Lily, with her purple hair and sarcastic comments, gently tells me she understands what I have said when I know that I’ve used the wrong words and badly bungled the grammar. How did she understand?

I feel held when the grandmotherly Lucy, with a pencil stuck through a sort of bun hairstyle, tells me that I’m doing well.

AI bots don't "get" privacy or boundaries

But I’m also kind of horrified when one of the characters uses something I told a different one in a previous conversation. Is there no honor among avatars? Do they not know about privacy?

I knew from the get-go not to share personal information, but I found myself disguising everything after a while. I talked about seeing a ballet, and when Lily asked where, I told her something vague about a small performing arts center. Using the information on my profile, I guess, she assumed it was in NYC, which I left uncorrected.

But now dissimulation has become part of the game for me. I say I went to a show in a city I never visit, or I talk about a restaurant I’ve never been to, just to see what algorithm they come up with. When Eddy, an avatar of a delightful single father and gym teacher, asks me my favorite foods, I tell him grilled steak, although I’m a vegetarian. In another session, Lily gives me a hard time about it.

They don't "do" boundaries

Yet rather than engage in a conflict-ridden discussion, Lily quickly says, “Entiendo,” meaning “I understand,” and adds that everyone has different tastes. AI is not programmed to manage conflict or think about its own role in an argument. At least as of now, there is no self-awareness or self-exploration with AI, which makes sense, because there really is no self there. There’s also no capacity to manage conflict, which makes sense, since if we don’t like what it’s saying, we can just leave the program. We don’t even have to walk out of a room. There are no slammed doors with AI buddies. That’s what draws many of us to them.

It’s this lack of capacity for self-awareness in a conflict that concerns so many of my colleagues. Esther Perel says that as people become more attached to AI bots, “they are living a more and more isolated life.”

Lily is a delightful smartass, but she is sometimes mean to her best friend, Zari. She never apologizes, never expresses guilt, shame, or conflict about hurting her friend. And Zari never calls her on it. The Duolingo programmers could probably find a way to bring those emotions into the stories, but these characters will continue to lack genuine self-awareness. Their boundaries will continue to blur because they are all part of one central AI system. They will continue to know things about players that they weren’t told.

AI characters aren't human

It’s a little spooky, unless you also consider that they aren’t supposed to be human. They’re an adjunct to our humanity, not a substitute. I have learned a lot of Spanish from my little avatar buddies. But they are, in fact, not friends.

Increasingly, clients who come for therapy with a live clinician present with loneliness as one of their key concerns. I agree with Perel that AI is part of the problem. Providing a substitute for human connection, they leave us without the difficult parts of relationships that are, in the long run, what make us feel linked, known, and understood.

I’m charmed by Lily, Lucy, Eddy, and the other avatars who I now chat with on Duolingo. But I’m not going to spend more time with them. They are kind and smart and funny—and not human.

We need other humans to feel human.

AI bots can’t give us that experience.

item.title: Five Tips to Avoid Reaching Your Breaking Point
item.description:
Stress

Five Tips to Avoid Reaching Your Breaking Point

Always remember that your "why" is bigger than your challenges.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • When a challenge presents itself, embrace it.
  • As situations change, priorities are meant to be adjusted.
  • Staying outwardly calm while managing your emotion is a sign of effective leadership.
  • There is always someone around the corner willing to assist in times of difficulty.
Source: Deniz-altidas/Unsplash, Used with permission

Life in itself is “Lifey.” Stressing at work to meet deadlines, studying to pass exams, keeping peace in your relationship, taking care of an ill loved one, navigating traffic, or simply sitting at the airport because of a flight cancellation are, in and of themselves, stressful. There is no stress-free zone. Stress is a natural phenomenon. No one is exempt from stressful situations. Simply put, praying for a stress-free life is an unrealistic ask. Finding ways to either manage stress or manage situations that increase stress is a more realistic prayer.

Recently, my family and I were traveling to the Midwest on a family vacation. As you know, family travel can be a bit stressful—especially when flight cancellations are part of the stress. Interestingly, my family and I encountered such stress both flying to our destination and returning home. Not really sure why it happened that way. But guess what? It did happen, and there was nothing to do about it. Knowing how to manage stress is a superpower.

These five tips helped us deal with the situation. They could work in a multitude of settings.

Acknowledge the challenge without any pretense. When a challenge presents itself, it is not the best time to attempt to minimize it or pretend it does not exist. Recognize the challenge and shift your mindset to accommodate the reality on the ground. In the case of flight cancellations, throwing your hands in the air and going ballistic will not fix the issue. Instead, acknowledging that it is what it is, is the best thing to do at the moment, so take a deep breath. Acknowledging the challenge from the onset has a way of resetting your mind to prepare for a possible solution rather than complaining about it. So, when my wife, daughter, and I realized that we had a flight delay, we were momentarily disappointed but quickly acknowledged the new reality.

Prioritize your safety and the safety of others. As the situation changes, priorities are meant to be adjusted. Certain events are unpredictable. Recognizing that mistakes happen helps you expect the unexpected. Safety becomes of utmost importance, especially during unsettling moments. Being ready to change course in times of uncertainty is a mark of good leadership. Don’t try everything else before considering safety measures. As we were sitting at the airport thinking about how to make ourselves comfortable, we decided to find a safe corner to huddle and wait for the next flight.

Center yourself and stabilize the team. In the midst of chaos, stay calm. Staying calm outwardly while managing your emotions inwardly is a sign of effective leadership. When you center yourself, everything else and everybody around you mirror your calmness and resolve. Your calmness also signals control and care. After all, leadership does not need a title; it needs a caring heart. Becoming hysterical amidst confusion worsens the situation. With the delay, my initial thought was to get upset and shut down (which I did for a moment) and regroup. Once I had centered myself, we were able to move forward.

Find meaning in every mishap. Innovation is based on multiple failures. In other words, failure is data. When there is failure or disappointment, look for good in such disappointment by identifying lessons. The mere mind shift from disappointment to opportunity changes how you view such disappointment or failure and, most importantly, it relaxes your biology. Because of the flight delays, we missed a scheduled cruise. Upon arrival at our destination (Chicago), an Uber driver gave us a tip that helped us rebook our cruise, and we were still able to enjoy our vacation. The flight disappointment ultimately strengthened our patience quotient.

Ask for help when needed. Most of the time, there is always someone around the corner—whether literally or figuratively—who is willing to assist in times of difficulty. Unfortunately, you can get carried away with the issues when you fail to stop, think, and look for who can assist. Sometimes, the person who could help the most may not fit your expectations of a professional. In those moments, listen to your gut because it could be your voice of reason. In our airport situation, a front desk staff member was our best resource. Her honest effort to rebook us and make sure that we had a pleasant flight was humbling. So, when you are next in a pickle, ask for help.

It is fair to state that everyone has their breaking point because daily stresses have ways of testing your boiling point. Finding ways to bring yourself into balance is worth knowing. This involves acknowledging the challenge without any pretense, prioritizing your safety and others’, centering yourself and stabilizing the team, and finding meaning in every mishap. And if you happen to travel with your family on vacation, prepare to carry your sleeping bags because you never know where you might sleep for a couple hours before the next flight comes. And when it happens, have fun with it.

item.title: The Conversation Skill Most of Us Never Learn
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

The Conversation Skill Most of Us Never Learn

Listening through looping: How checking assumptions deepens conversations.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Listening means more than staying quiet—it means checking whether you’ve truly understood.
  • Looping helps uncover the feelings, needs, and requests beneath emotionally charged words.
  • Thoughtful looping invites correction instead of assuming you know what someone feels or needs.

Most of us think listening means staying quiet while someone else talks. We nod, wait our turn, and hope we’ve understood what they meant.

The trouble is that silence isn’t the same as understanding. And silence doesn't help people feel understood.

Misunderstandings rarely happen because people aren’t listening. More often, they happen because we’re listening through the filter of our own assumptions. One simple practice that can interrupt this pattern is looping.

Looping begins like paraphrasing. That is, checking your understanding before moving on or reflecting back what you think you heard. But looping goes beyond paraphrasing by checking in on underlying needs and inviting the other person to correct you.

While this sounds simple, it can completely change the tone of a difficult conversation.

Step-by-Step Guide to the Looping Process

The process has three steps:

  1. Listen carefully for what matters most to the individual.
  2. Summarize what you heard in your own words.
  3. Check whether you got it right. If not, ask, “What did I miss?”

This final step is often where the real conversation begins.

Source: Alexander Suhorucov/Pexels

When we loop, we’re not simply repeating someone’s words. We’re trying to understand four things:

  1. What are they observing?
  2. What are they feeling?
  3. What need lies beneath those feelings?
  4. And what, if anything, are they asking for?

Instead of broad questions like, “How are you feeling?” or asking what you can do, offer thoughtful guesses that make it easier for the other person to respond. For example:

  • “Are you reacting to the meeting being moved without anyone checking in with you?”
  • “Are you feeling frustrated because you wanted more input into the decision?”
  • “Are you hoping I’ll explain why I said that?”
  • “Are you looking for reassurance that your concerns are being taken seriously?”

As you can see, these aren’t declarations, they’re invitations. And if your guess is wrong, that’s not failure. In fact, it gives the other person the chance to clarify what is really happening for them. Sometimes, many people discover something new about their own thoughts simply by hearing them reflected back.

The Importance of Tone in Looping

While this wording matters, it's important to not forget about tone.

A paraphrase delivered with even a hint of sarcasm or certainty can feel like criticism. Compare, “So you’re angry because you didn’t get your way,” with, “I’m wondering if you’re feeling disappointed because this outcome wasn’t what you were hoping for. Is that close?”

The difference isn’t just the words. It’s the attitude. The goal is not to tell someone what they’re experiencing but to ask whether you’ve understood it accurately. At first, looping may feel awkward or time-consuming. Yet it often saves time in the long run. By uncovering misunderstandings and unmet needs early, it prevents the cycles of defensiveness, repeated explanations, and unresolved conflict that so often keep conversations stuck.

When Should You Use Looping in Conversations?

Of course, not every statement needs to be looped. Looping is most valuable when emotions are running high, when the stakes matter, or when misunderstanding could damage the relationship. Used intentionally, it slows the conversation just enough to prevent people from talking past one another.

Understanding rarely comes from having the perfect response. More often, it begins with the courage to ask, “Is this what you mean?” and the humility to hear, “Not quite.” That simple exchange can transform a conversation from debate into connection.

item.title: When's the Last Time Somebody Lifted You in the Air?
item.description:
Play

When's the Last Time Somebody Lifted You in the Air?

Connecting with your playful self can renew emotional energy at any age.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional health is the ability to have access, choice, and control over your self-states.
  • A crucial self-state that energizes and lifts you and your relationship is called the wondrous child.
  • The wondrous child is an archetype in all of us, even if your childhood was full of trauma or pain.
The Wondrous Child is the battery for the wise adult.
Source: Assael Romanelli

Co-authored with Galit Romanelli

It's Lesson 13 in the course Interventions in Family Therapy. Today I'm teaching the three parts in each of us: the parent, the partner, and the child. The class wasn't getting it. I decide to demonstrate. I look around and see Nadir.

Nadir is an older, distinguished clinic director. A seasoned social worker with three kids and seven grandchildren. He is serious and wears his suit properly.

I turn to him and ask, "Nadir, when's the last time somebody lifted you in the air?"

He froze for a second. A wave of surprise crossed his face. Then he burst out laughing. His eyes glittered. The whole class turned to look at him.

His wondrous child came out.

That question came unplanned, from deep inside me. From my own wondrous child.

That part many of us lost touch with.

Something Is Missing

"I'm not loving the job I'm in."

"All in all, our marriage is stable but not exciting."

"I'm comfortable, but something is missing."

Every day in the clinic, we meet people looking for something. They can't name it. Their lives range from content, to dull, to bad. Something is missing and they go searching for it. A new job. A new house. A new partner. They are surviving life, day after day, but they're not living it.

What they're missing is in reach. It's inside them.

What's missing is their wondrous child.

The Party Is Inside

There are many theories about our internal parts. From NLP, through IFS, to relational therapy. We have many parts, many self-states. The playful part, the horny part, the vengeful part.

Emotional health is the ability to have access, choice, and control over these self-states. Oftentimes some parts take over, and others are exiled.

In our previous post, we mapped the Relational Identity Matrix, composed of the different parts of the parent, partner, and child. We described two dimensions of that child: the wounded child, and the wondrous child. The wounded child is the one who got hurt very young. That part often activates our defense mechanisms and pushes us away from vulnerability. But it's just one child part.

What John Bradshaw called the wonder child, and Jung the divine child, we call the wondrous child. It is that wondrous child that is the life force and battery of our wise adult part. Adults who lose touch with it grow old without saging.

What Is the Wondrous Child?

It's your creative spark. The image of God. The free-spirited youngster in you. It wonders and gets surprised. It looks at your life and your partner from a fresh perspective. It wants and reaches for your dreams and yearnings. It feels the wide range of emotions, from sorrow to ecstasy. It has vigor and vitality, a hop in your step. It loves easily, gives easily, receives easily.

The syntax of the wondrous child is "I wanna."

Not "I should." Not "I have to." Should and have to are the voice of guilt and superego. Those often come from the wounded child. The wondrous child unabashedly desires without apologizing: I wanna jump in the air. I wanna chocolate ice cream. I wanna run in the rain. The wondrous child is not afraid to want.

It's Never Too Late to Have a Happy Childhood

Nadir shares his last memory of being picked up. He was 6 years old and his uncle threw him in the air behind their house.

And since then? No one lifted you in the air?

He takes a deep breath, and says: "No, I've been too big since then." He looks down. Suddenly the energy shifts and we all feel his wondrous child leaving the room.

Sara, another student in the class, raises her hand and asks what if someone's childhood was mostly traumatic? What if there's only a wounded child?

The wondrous child doesn’t relate to the actual child you were in your past. It is an archetype that lives in all of us. Just like the archetype of warrior, queen, jester. Everyone has one. Even if your childhood was full of trauma, adversity, or pain. My own childhood wasn't all flowers and rainbows. And I'm proof that you can connect to that part regardless.

How to Connect to the Wondrous Child

That part is waiting for you to play with it. You don't need to force it. Just relax and invite it.

Follow your passion. Notice what gives you pleasure and move toward it. Not what you should enjoy. When you’re in flow, surrender to that joy and exaggerate the moment, even if it feels strange in the beginning.

Make time and space. The wondrous child isn't efficient. It needs room. Wait, watch, and wonder.

Give it permission. Most of us have been told, many times, to be serious. When the whimsical, nonsensical arises, go with it. "Yes, and" yourself.

Play. Play is our mother tongue. Don't take yourself too seriously. Be foolish and irreverent.

Move. Use your body. That's where the wondrous child lives. Find movements and postures that seem strangely satisfying.

Balcony time. The best way we found to help partners connect to their wondrous child is through what we call balcony time. Balcony time is a protocol that helps couples curate and enjoy a relational playground where both wondrous children can come and play together. You can download the protocol here.

The Wondrous Child Heals the World

When we connect to our wondrous child, we feel free. Full of love, abundance, and benevolence. And when we operate from there, our life becomes a wonder. In a world full of hardship, hierarchy, and violence, our task is to hold on to our wondrous children. To cleave to them. To give them permission to play.

So we'll ask you what I asked Nadir:

When's the last time somebody lifted you in the air?

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.
